1.pericope_label: The priests are barred from the holy things while unclean

schools.summary: Calvin explains why a rule already binding on all Israel had to be re-enacted for the priests, since men in honour make God's favour a pretext and dignity a cover for scandal, so that their office binds them harder rather than excusing them; Gill distinguishes blemish from impurity and supplies Jarchi's measure of what defiles.

Henry sorts the defilements into lasting and passing, holds that what merely excluded a layman made a priest abominable, reads nearness to God as exposure rather than security, and warns against profaning God's name in the very things we hallow to him.

Clarke reads the chapter as requiring perfection in the offering as well as the offerer; Wesley takes the cutting off for excommunication from both administering and partaking, and explains that the priest's penalty was no longer than a layman's because the holy things were his subsistence.

Keil and Delitzsch enumerate the defilements and narrow the holy things to the heave- and wave-offerings assigned for the priests' maintenance; Ellicott links the chapter to the close of the previous one, corrects two renderings, notes that the formula 'cut off from my presence' occurs nowhere else in the Pentateuch, and reports the second Temple's reading of the death threatened as inflicted by heaven.

debates: Why a law already given to all Israel needed re-enacting for the priests, and why their penalty was no heavier
outliers: Ellicott observes that Leviticus elsewhere always says 'cut off from his people' and here alone 'from my presence'

10.pericope_label: Who may eat of the holy things, and restitution for eating them unwittingly

schools.summary: Calvin argues the law was aimed less at strangers than at priestly avarice, which would have turned the offerings into a trade and the priest's house into a provision-market, asks why the priests should be compensated by a man who ate unwittingly, and reads the closing warning as addressed to priests whose impiety as mediators brings guilt on everyone; Gill identifies the stranger as any non-Aaronite and prefers marriage to purchase as the reason the priest's wife may eat.

Henry sorts the household by permanence rather than presence, reads the widow's return as the widows' God not leaving her comfortless, takes the bearing of iniquity as a warning against any mediator besides Christ, and ends on David and the shewbread as proof that rituals give way to morals.

Clarke identifies the sojourner and hired servant from Jewish usage, uses the bought slave's standing in the priestly family to attack European Christians who cite this law to justify slavery, and reports from Ward that Bengali widows still return to their fathers; Wesley explains that a wife passes into her husband's privileges and that restitution is of the equivalent.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the slave's right in circumcision and the daughter's in household membership rather than descent; Ellicott defines the classes of servant, extends the privilege as the second Temple did, limits the returning widow to the heave-offerings, reports two later rulings about her, and weighs the fifth part against the heavier penalty for withholding.

debates: Whether the closing warning about bearing iniquity is addressed to the priests or to the people
outliers: Henry offers a second reading of 'bear the iniquity of trespass', taking it of the priests' mediatorial eating of the sin-offering rather than of a stranger's guilt

17.pericope_label: Every sacrifice to be without blemish, from Israelite and stranger alike

schools.summary: Calvin rejects the rendering 'at your own will' for one pointing to God's good pleasure, then allows the other sense if taken of gratuitous favour and ends on Christ washing out the blemishes of regenerate offerings; he decides against the rabbinic reading of the stranger's hand and explains why the sacrifices are called the bread of God. Gill shows the demand for unblemished victims was shared by Egyptians, Romans and Greeks.

Henry catalogues the blemishes, reads the vow-and-freewill distinction as teaching exactness in performing what we have promised, and turns the law into type, the unblemished victim prefiguring the Lamb without blemish whom Pilate pronounced faultless without knowing it.

Clarke glosses the terms for the superfluous and the lacking as monstrosity in either direction and reports the Jewish view that such animals never reached the altar but were sold for the sanctuary; Wesley notes the male was required for the burnt offering alone.

Keil and Delitzsch state the rule, argue against Clericus and Knobel that the closing clause forbids castration itself rather than the preparing of sacrifices, and ground the prohibition in the mutilation of God's creation; Ellicott matches the animals' blemishes to the priests', corrects several renderings, judges the text of the freewill concession probably disarranged, and notes the gelding prohibition still binds Jewish farmers.

debates: Whether a disproportioned animal could really be offered as a freewill gift, and whether the stranger's hand means a Gentile offerer or an imported beast
outliers: Ellicott proposes that the verse permitting a freewill offering is textually disarranged and originally forbade it, against the plain sense the other sources accept

26.pericope_label: The age of the offering, the dam and her young, and the closing charge

schools.summary: Calvin dismisses the creation-week explanation of the eighth day as too subtle and rests on maturity, finds fraud and cruelty alike in a victim taken from the womb, argues the dam-and-young rule is primarily about sacrifice while insisting God's altar should not be a Cyclopean slaughter-house, and makes every human invention in worship a profanation of God's name; Gill reports the rabbinic limitation of the rule to the female.

Clarke protests that a bullock was never brought forth and the word means a calf, restrained from correcting the text only by his rule of printing the common version exactly, grounds the mercy rule in not blunting our moral feelings, and objects again to the translators over the phrase children of Israel; Wesley reads the hallowing as either Israel keeping God's commands or God executing his judgments upon them.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the seven days by the creature's immaturity, cite the comparable Roman intervals, and ground the dam-and-young rule in the relation God established between parent and offspring; Ellicott reports two second-Temple rulings on the wording, quotes the Chaldee's call to be merciful as the Father in heaven is merciful, and complains that the conjunctions of the closing charge are mistranslated in a way that mars the dignity of the original.

debates: Why the eighth day was appointed, and whether the dam-and-young rule governs sacrifice or ordinary slaughter
outliers: Calvin rejects as too subtle the very reason Keil and Delitzsch give for the eighth day, that the week is the period sanctified by creation
